title: Conditionals in CuTe DSL
key_concepts: Runtime conditionals are evaluated on the GPU
Runtime conditionals include both branches in generated code
Avoid warp divergence for better performance
critical_patterns: Activation Functions: Compile-time dispatch for different activations
Precision Selection: Compile-time choice between FP16 and FP32
Bounds Checking: Runtime checks for safe data access
Warp Divergence Mitigation: Use predicated execution to minimize divergence
constraints: Cannot use return, raise, or pass in dynamic conditionals
Variables defined in if block are not available outside
Cannot change variable type within conditionals
Runtime values cannot be used with cutlass.const_expr
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL supports both runtime and compile-time conditionals, allowing for flexible and optimized GPU kernel code generation. Runtime conditionals are evaluated on the GPU, keeping both branches in the generated code, which can lead to warp divergence if not managed carefully. Compile-time conditionals, using cutlass.const_expr, are evaluated during JIT compilation, resulting in only the taken branch being included in the final code, thus eliminating dead code and improving performance. Key patterns include activation functions, precision selection, and bounds checking, each leveraging compile-time evaluation to optimize execution paths. Constraints include the prohibition of return, raise, or pass statements within dynamic conditionals, and the necessity to define variables outside conditionals if they are needed later. Additionally, variable types cannot change within conditionals, and runtime values are incompatible with cutlass.const_expr. To minimize warp divergence, predicated execution or structuring work so entire warps take the same path is recommended. Understanding when to use runtime versus compile-time conditionals is crucial for achieving optimal performance and code efficiency in CuTe DSL.
